analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for regulators to put big nonbank financial firms under stricter federal supervision.
analysis.headline: Backed by just four House members — two Democrats and two Republicans — the bill never got a hearing or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Financial Stability Oversight Council is a panel of regulators that can designate a big nonbank financial firm — an insurer, asset manager, or similar company — for Federal Reserve supervision and stricter safety rules. This bill would force the council, before making such a designation, to first conclude that milder steps — including new standards or a plan submitted by the company itself — could not fix the risk. The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee and never advanced; it expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Large nonbank financial companies — insurers, mutual fund and asset managers, and other financial firms outside the banking system. They could avoid, or at least delay, Federal Reserve supervision and tougher capital and liquidity standards, and they would gain a formal seat at the table in the process of deciding whether they get regulated. Banks already face those standards, so unregulated nonbank rivals would also gain a competitive edge.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large nonbank insurers and asset managers

how_it_helps.text: A nonbank financial company could escape designation for Federal Reserve supervision whenever the council finds that some alternative — new standards, safeguards, or a written plan the company submits — would be enough to contain the threat, rather than being designated outright.

The bill gives the company itself a consultative role in its own designation: the council must work 'in consultation with the company' and consider actions 'by the company under a written plan' before voting to regulate it, raising the burden on regulators.

Because these heightened standards apply only to nonbank firms, banks would keep their existing rules while nonbank rivals that avoid designation would operate under lighter oversight, a relative competitive advantage for both.

analysis.who_pays: The public. The designation process exists to catch nonbank giants whose failure could destabilize the financial system — the kind of firm whose collapse in 2008 (AIG) forced a government rescue. Making designation harder means weaker oversight of exactly those firms, with the residual risk of a bailout landing on taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, if a risky nonbank fails

drawbacks.text: The bill forces the council to exhaust alternative steps before it can designate a firm, which could cost valuable time while a company's risk is still building — precisely when quick, decisive oversight matters most.
It lets the company being scrutinized help shape the decision about whether it should be regulated, submitting its own plan and consulting on the alternative, which tilts the process toward the firm.

Supporters of strong oversight would object that the 2008 AIG rescue showed why nonbank designation authority matters; a 2010-law reform that makes that authority harder to use shifts the cost of a future failure onto the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim — making the council consider less intrusive options before designating a firm — is a defensible process reform, and it drew support from both parties. But the cost side is heavier: it hands the regulated company a role in its own designation, raises the burden on regulators, and weakens the main tool Congress created after 2008 to police systemically risky firms outside the banking system. The savings to the firms would come at the expense of the public's protection against another taxpayer-financed rescue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the chair never brought it up for action, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Foster introduced the bill on June 15, 2021, joined by Reps. Perlmutter (D), Hollingsworth (R), and Huizenga (R).
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The action history shows nothing after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public and financial regulators came out ahead: the existing authority to designate risky nonbank firms for Federal Reserve supervision stays intact rather than being harder to use. Large nonbank financial firms, who would have gained a say in their own oversight, lost the chance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulators kept their unweakened designation authority

for.name: Rep. Bill Foster
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring the council to consider alternatives before designating a nonbank firm for Fed supervision

against.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing, markup, or floor action; the record shows only a referral

sides.party_line_note: The bill had genuinely mixed-party backing — two Democrats and two Republicans — but with only four supporters and no votes ever taken, no partisan pattern ever emerged.

industries.industry: Large nonbank financial companies (insurers, asset managers)
industries.note: The bill would let these firms avoid or delay Federal Reserve supervision and stricter safety standards by proposing their own alternative fixes, and gives them a consultative role in the decision. Their gain is reduced oversight of the very risks that, if realized, land on taxpayers.

The heightened standards at issue apply only to nonbank firms, so banks that remain subject to them would face unregulated or lightly regulated nonbank competitors on more even terms. This is a relative advantage, not a change in banks' own rules.
